Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 59, verse 1–2:

(p-259) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah al-Hashr (The Gathering)

This surah is Madinan by the consensus of the people of knowledge, and it is the surah of Banu al-Nadir. That is because "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had made a treaty of peace with Banu al-Nadir, and they considered that no banner of his would be turned back. But when the defeat at Uhud occurred, they doubted, sided secretly with Quraysh, and betrayed. When the Prophet ﷺ returned from Uhud, the stance of Banu al-Nadir, their betrayal of his covenant and their alliance with the disbelievers became clear to him. He gathered against them, besieged them, and made a covenant with them that they would leave their land. So they departed for various lands: Khaybar, al-Sham and other lands. Then came the matter of Banu Qurayzah, which was a sequel to the Confederates."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering. You did not think they would leave, and they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah. But Allah came at them from where they did not expect, and He cast terror into their hearts. They destroyed their houses by their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take warning, O people of insight.﴾

The discussion has already preceded concerning the glorification of inanimate things covered by the generality of "whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth," and that the people of knowledge differed on this. Some said it is literal, while others said it is metaphorical, meaning that the traces of creation and origination in them are like glorification and a call to glorification from whoever is able to glorify. Makki said: "sabbaha" means prayed and prostrated. All of this carries the meaning of submission and voluntary obedience. "The Mighty, the Wise" are two attributes fitting what comes afterward of the story of the enemy whom He expelled from their homes.

Those "who disbelieved among the People of the Book" are Banu al-Nadir. They were a great tribe of the Children of Israel, equal in rank and standing to Banu Qurayzah. The two tribes were called "the two priests," because they were descended from the priest Ibn Harun. Their land and fortresses were near Madinah, and they had palm groves (p-260) and great wealth. "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned from Uhud, he went out to Banu al-Nadir, besieged them, and expelled them on condition that they carry away of their property what the camels could bear, except the armour—that is, all the weapons—so they departed for various lands." This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes.﴾

As for His saying, "at the first gathering" (li-awwali al-hashr), the people differed about its meaning, although they agreed that "al-hashr" means gathering and driving toward a certain direction. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others said: it means the gathering of the Resurrection, i.e., this is its first stage, and rising from the graves is its last. It is narrated from al-Hasan that the Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Proceed, this is the first of the gathering, and we are following in its footsteps." Ikrimah, al-Zuhri and others said: the meaning is "to the first place of gathering," which is al-Sham, because most of Banu al-Nadir went to al-Sham. It has been narrated that the gathering of the Resurrection is toward al-Sham, and that the Prophet ﷺ "said to Banu al-Nadir: 'Go out!' They said: 'To where, O Muhammad?' He said: 'To the land of the gathering.'" Some said—in the book of al-Mahdawi—that what is intended is the gathering in this world, which is the exile and expulsion. So what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did to Banu al-Nadir is its first, and what Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) did to the people of Khaybar is its last. The verse conveys an unseen matter, and the Prophet ﷺ had foretold the exile of the people of Khaybar. It may also be that it is the last gathering, in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ during his illness: "Let there not remain two religions in the Arabian Peninsula," for that includes the expulsion of their remnants. Al-Khalil, as related by al-Zajjaj, said: it was called a peninsula (jazirah) because the Sea of Abyssinia, the Persian Gulf, the Tigris and the Euphrates surround it. In this surrounding there is room for scrutiny.

His saying: ﴿You did not think they would leave﴾ means: because of their might and the greatness of their number. Your hopes and assumptions did not reach the point that they would leave and abandon their property to you. In accordance with that degree of might, numbers and fortification, they thought that Allah would not overcome them. His saying "from Allah" means: from the army of Allah and the party of Allah. His saying: ﴿But Allah came at them from where they did not expect﴾ is an expression for Allah Most High making the Muslims prevail over them and placing them in the sphere of defeat and humiliation. The majority of readers read "al-ru'b" (p-261) with a sukun on the ayn, while Abu Ja'far and Shaybah read "al-ru'ub" with a damma on the ayn.

The commentators differed about the meaning of His saying: ﴿They destroyed their houses by their own hands and the hands of the believers.﴾ Al-Dahhak, al-Zajjaj and others said: whenever the Muslims demolished part of their fortifications in the fighting, they themselves demolished parts of the houses and repaired the fort continually; this is the meaning of their destroying. Al-Zuhri and others said: when it was permitted to them to take whatever the camels could carry, they would leave no good piece of wood, no beam, no pillar, without pulling it out, and they destroyed the houses behind them. His saying: ﴿and the hands of the believers﴾ refers to the fact that their own deeds of disbelief were a cause for the believers to destroy their houses, so it is as if they had destroyed them by the hands of the believers. A group of the exegetes said: when they resolved on departure, they were stingy about leaving the houses intact for the believers, so they demolished and destroyed them out of a desire to cause corruption for whoever would come after. Qatadah said: the believers destroyed from outside in order to enter, and they destroyed from inside. The majority of reciters read "yukhribuna" with a sukun on the kha and a light ra, while Abu 'Amr alone, al-Hasan (according to one report from him), Qatadah and Isa read "yukharribuna" with a fatha on the kha and a shadda on the ra. A group of the linguists said: the two readings have one meaning. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: "kharib" means he demolished and corrupted, while "akhrab" means he left the place in ruin and departed from it.

Then Blessed and Most High alerted the believers and others who are able to look, to the support of His Messenger ﷺ and His act on his behalf against those who opposed and confronted him, by His saying: ﴿So take warning, O people of insight﴾, i.e., the minds and understandings.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 59, verses 3–6:**

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Had Allah not decreed exile for them, He would have punished them in this world; and for them in the Hereafter is the punishment of the Fire.﴾ ﴿That is because they opposed Allah and His Messenger; and whoever opposes Allah, then Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down, or left standing on their roots, it was by the permission of Allah, and so that He might disgrace the defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And whatever Allah restored (as fayʾ) to His Messenger from them, you did not spur horses or camels against it; but Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾

In this verse, the Exalted informs that He decreed exile (jalāʾ) for the Children of Israel. The Banu al-Nadir were among those who settled in the Hijaz shortly after the death of Musa, peace be upon him, because they were among the army that returned after disobeying in not killing the boy, the son of the king of the Amalekites, for the sake of his camels and his wealth. Musa, peace be upon him, had said to them: "Do not spare anyone." When that army returned to the Children of Israel in Syria, they found Musa dead. The Children of Israel said to them: "You are disobedient. By Allah, you will not enter our lands upon us." The people of that army said to the Children of Israel: "We have no preference other than the lands whose people we conquered." So they departed to the Hijaz and remained there. The exile that Bukhtnassar imposed on the people of Syria did not befall them. Allah, the Exalted, had decreed exile for the Children of Israel, and this exile befell them at the hands of Muhammad (ﷺ). Had it not been so, Allah would have punished them in this world by the sword and killing, as He did with the people of Badr and others. It is said: "Jalā al-rajul" (the man went into exile), and "ajlāhu ghayruhu" (another exiled him), and it may be said: "ajlā al-rajul nafsahu" (the man exiled himself), with the same meaning as "jalā."

And *al-mushāqqa* (opposition) means that a person is on one side and his opponent is on the other side.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down﴾, its occasion was that some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) placed their hands upon the palm trees of the Banu al-Nadir, cutting and burning them. The Banu al-Nadir said: "What is this corruption, O Muhammad, when you forbid corruption?" Some of the Companions then refrained from this, and that was at the beginning of the war with them. So the verse was revealed informing that everything that occurred, whether cutting or leaving, was by the permission of Allah, the Exalted. The verse answered the statement of the Banu al-Nadir that Muhammad forbids corruption yet here he is causing corruption. Allah, the Exalted, informed them that this was by His permission, and that He might disgrace by it the defiantly disobedient among the Banu al-Nadir.

People differed about the meaning of *al-līna*. Al-Hasan, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and ʿAmr ibn Maymun said: *al-līna* is the palm tree; they are two names with one meaning, and its plural is *līn* and *liyān*. A poet said:

> A long-necked she-camel like the tall palm trees, in whom the fierce one kindled the flames.

And another said:

> The flight-feathers of a bird of prey, resting upon a palm tree, its feathers glistening with the dew of its night.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and a group of the linguists said: *al-līna* among the palm trees is that which is not *ʿajwa* (a type of dates). Sufyan ibn Saʿid al-Thawri said: *al-līna* is the noble (choice) palm tree. Abu ʿUbayda, according to what is narrated from him, and Sufyan said: *al-līna* is that whose dates are *lawn*, which is a type of date called *al-lawn*. Sufyan said: it is intensely yellow, transparent so that its pit is seen from outside. Its original form is *liwna*, but it was changed to *līna* to harmonize with the kasra. Abu ʿUbayda also said: *al-līn* is the mixed colors of palm trees which contain no *ʿajwa* nor seeds.

Ibn Masʿud and al-Aʿmash read: ﴿or left them standing upon their roots (*qawwaman*)﴾ [instead of *qāʾiman*].

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿And whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them﴾, the verse... is an informing that what was taken from the Banu al-Nadir and from Fadak is specifically for the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is not under the ruling of *ghanīma* (spoils of war) which is obtained by spurring horses and fighting, but under the ruling of the one-fifth of spoils (*khums*). This is because the Banu al-Nadir were not subdued by spurring horses and camels, and they were not fought with a great battle. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took from it for himself the provision of his household, and he distributed the rest among the Emigrants (*muhājirūn*), and the Helpers (*anṣār*) were not given anything, except that Abu Dujana Simak ibn Kharasha and Sahl ibn Hunayf complained of great poverty, so he gave to them both. This is the statement of a group of scholars. Concerning this, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The wealth of the Banu al-Nadir was among what Allah, the Exalted, restored to His Messenger (ﷺ), which the Muslims did not spur horses or camels against. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would spend from it on his family for a year's provision, and what remained of it he placed in weapons and horses as preparation in the way of Allah, the Exalted."

Some scholars said: Likewise, everything that was conquered by the leaders (*a’immah*) without spurring against it belongs to them exclusively. *Al-wajīf* is less than *al-taḍrīb* (galloping hard). It is said: "wajafa al-furs" (the horses charged) and "awjafahu al-rākib" (the rider made it charge). *Al-ījāf* is speed of travel and striving in it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 59, verses 7–8:

His, the Exalted and Majestic's, saying:

﴿Whatever Allah has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns belongs to Allah, to the Messenger, to the kinsmen (of the Prophet), the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer, so that it does not circulate only among the rich among you. Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it. And fear Allah; indeed Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ ﴿(It is) for the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from Allah and His pleasure, and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful.﴾

The people of the towns mentioned in this verse are the people of al-Safra', Yanbu', Wadi al-Qura, and the Arab towns there which are called the Arab towns (qura 'arabiyya). Their ruling differs from that of Banu al-Nadir. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not withhold anything of these for himself; rather he allowed them to be given to others. That is because they were conquered at that time. People differed about the manner of their conquest. It was said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) campaigned against them and sent a force to every place, and they obeyed, and he gave their people (the land) as a result. So it was among what was not gained by horses and camels (ma lam yujif 'alayhi), and its ruling was the ruling of spoils of war (ghanaʼim). On this interpretation there is no abrogation (naskh) in the verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave all of that to the emigrants and gave the Helpers (al-Ansar) none of it.

Qatada and Yazid ibn Ruman said: these towns were gained by horses and camels, but this is the ruling for what is so gained. Then Allah the Exalted abrogated this ruling by the verse of al-Anfal, placing in it the one-fifth (khums) for these categories, and the remaining four-fifths for the fighters. The verse of this surah did not contain a share for the fighters. This view is weak, because the verse of al-Anfal was revealed right after Badr, before Banu al-Nadir and a year and more before the matter of these towns. And "the kinsmen" in this verse refers to the relatives of the Prophet (ﷺ). They (the Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib) had withheld the zakat, so they were compensated from the fay'.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿so that it does not circulate only among the rich among you﴾, it is addressed to the Helpers, because there was no rich person among the emigrants at that time. The majority of reciters read "yakun" with the letter ya'. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Ja'far, and Hisham on the authority of Ibn 'Amir read it with the letter ta', and it is the complete (tamma) use of "kana" (meaning "to occur/happen"). The majority of reciters read "dulatan" with a damma on the dal and a fatha on the ha'. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "dawlatan" with a fatha on the dal and a fatha on the ha'. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Hisham on the authority of Ibn 'Amir read "dulatun" with a damma on the dal and on the ha'. 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: they both have one meaning. Al-Kisa'i and the expert analysts said: the fatha (dawla) refers to the sovereignty (mulk) with a damma on the mim (i.e. dawla as a "fi'la" of time), because it is an occurrence in time, while the damma (dulla) refers to possession (milk) with a kasra on the mim. The meaning is that they are like loans that the rich pass around among themselves through their dealings, while the needy are left with nothing. And there is no share in any of this property for a wealthy orphan or a wayfarer who has property present. The discussion of spoils has already passed in the commentary on surah [al-Anfal].

It is narrated that some of the Helpers spoke about these conquered towns and said: "We have our share of them." So there was revealed His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾, the verse... as a corrective and a deterrent in that matter. Then the meaning of the verse extended to the commands and prohibitions of the Prophet (ﷺ), to the point that some people said: wine is forbidden in the Book of Allah the Exalted by this verse. And Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, derived from it the curse upon the woman who tattoos and the woman who has herself tattooed... the hadith. He also saw a man in sewn garments while in the state of ihram and said to him: "Take this off you." The man said to him: "Do you recite to me a verse from the Book of Allah the Exalted for that?" Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Yes," and he recited this verse.

His, the Exalted's, saying: "for the poor emigrants" is an explanation of His saying: ﴿the needy and the wayfarer﴾. So He repeated the preposition lam of genitive, since the first (category) was in the genitive with the lam, to make clear that the substitution (badal) is from them. Then the Exalted described them with the attribute that entails their poverty and requires compassion for them, which is their expulsion from their homes and their properties. All the emigrants were either expelled by the disbelievers, or the circumstances of the disbelievers and their dominance and the imposition of emigration at that time (compelled them). He described them as poor even though some of them had some property, and this is the linguistic sense of poverty (hal al-faqr fi al-lugha). The explanation of this has already passed in the commentary on surah [al-Kahf]. His, the Exalted's, saying: "seeking" (yabtaghun) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). "Bounty" (fadl) and "pleasure" (ridwan) are meant to refer to the Hereafter and Paradise. The "support of Allah" is the support of His law and of His Prophet (ﷺ).

"The truthful" (al-sadiqun) in this verse combines truthfulness of speech and truthfulness of deeds, because their deeds in the matter of their emigration were in accordance with their words.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 59, verses 9–10:

The Most High said:

﴿And those who had settled in the abode [of faith] and in belief before them love those who emigrate to them, and find no need in their breasts for what they have been given, and prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves are in need. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful.﴾ ﴿And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and put no resentment in our hearts toward those who believe. Our Lord, You are indeed Kind and Merciful."﴾

"Alladhina tabawwa'u" (those who settled) refers to the Ansar (the Helpers of Madina). The pronoun in "qablihim" (before them) refers to the Muhajirun (the Emigrants). "Al-dar" (the abode) is Madina. The meaning is: they settled in the abode together with belief, and with this connection the meaning of the Most High's words "min qablihim" (before them) is correct, so reflect on it. Belief is not something one can "settle in," because it is not a place. But this is from eloquent speech, and it can be explained in several ways, all of which are beautiful and good.

In this verse Allah the Most High praised the Ansar for loving the Muhajirun, may Allah be pleased with all of them, for preferring them over themselves, and for having been protected from the stinginess of their own souls. This is because the implication of the Most High's words, ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾, is that these praised people have been protected from stinginess.

"Al-hajah" (need) here means envy. This was said by al-Hasan. It then covers all the aspects that are contrary to what the Prophet (ﷺ) did in giving the Muhajirun the wealth of Bani al-Nadir and the villages. "Utu" (were given) means "were given." The raised pronoun in "utu," whose subject is not named, refers to the Muhajirun.

The Most High's words, ﴿and prefer them over themselves﴾, up to the end of the verse, describe the Ansar. It has been narrated, through more than one chain, that it was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar. Abu al-Mutawakkil said: he was Thabit ibn Qays. Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said in the book of Makki: the kunya (honorific nickname) of this man was Abu Talha. Al-Mahdawi confused the account of this man: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called for hosting an emigrant, and an Ansari responded, though he had no wealth. He took the guest away and said to his wife, 'This is the guest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' She said, 'By Allah, I have nothing except the food of the children.' He said to her, 'Put your children to sleep, extinguish the lamp, and offer what you have to the guest, and let him think that we are eating.' They did that, and when he went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the morning, he said, 'Allah was amazed at your deed last night,' and the verse was revealed concerning that."

Preferring others over oneself is the most noble of character. Hudhayfa al-'Adawi said: On the day of Yarmuk I was searching among the wounded for a cousin of mine, and I had some water with me. I found him and said, "Shall I give you a drink?" He gestured yes. Then a man was crying "Ah!" My cousin gestured that I should go to him. It was Hisham ibn al-'As. I said, "Will you drink?" Then another was saying "Ah!" Hisham gestured that I should go to him. I came to him and found that his soul had departed. I returned to Hisham and found that he had died. I returned to my cousin and found that he too had died. I was amazed at their preference for others, may Allah the Most High have mercy on them. Abu Zayd al-Bistami said: A young man from Balkh came to us and said to me, "What is the limit of asceticism (zuhd) among you?" I said, "When we lose something, we are patient, and when we find something, we give thanks." He said, "This is the state of dogs among us in Balkh." I said, "Then what is asceticism among you?" He said, "When we lose something, we give thanks, and when we find something, we prefer others."

It has also been narrated that the cause of this verse was: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) divided these villages among the Muhajirun, he said to the Ansar, 'If you wish, you may divide among the Muhajirun from your wealth and homes, and share with them in this spoil,' and then this verse was revealed."

"Al-khasasah" (poverty) means destitution and need. It is derived from "khasa'is al-bayt" (the gaps of a house), which are the openings and spaces that remain between its wooden sticks. Thus the state of the poor person is similar: deficiency and need pass through it. "Shuhh al-nafs" (stinginess of the soul) is the intensity of its greed, its clinging to wealth, its desire for it, and the extension of hope. This is the essence of stinginess of the soul, and it is the source of every bad character trait. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever pays the obligatory zakat, hospitably hosts the guest, and gives in times of calamity, has been freed from stinginess."

People differed after what we have said. The majority and those knowledgeable in theology (al-kalam) went along with this. According to this interpretation, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, may Allah be pleased with him, used to circumambulate the Ka'ba saying, "O Allah, protect me from the stinginess of my soul," and nothing more. He was asked about this and said, "If You grant it to me, I will not commit any evil."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The stinginess of the soul is a poverty that the wealth of money does not remove; rather, it increases it and makes it worse.

Ibn Zayd, Ibn Jubayr and a group said: Whoever does not take what Allah the Most High has forbidden him, and does not withhold the obligatory zakat, has been freed from the stinginess of the soul. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The stinginess of the soul is consuming the property of others unjustly. As for a person withholding his own property, that is miserliness (bukhl). It is ugly, but it is not stinginess (shuhh)." 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, recited "shuhhi" with a kasra on the shin. "Yuwaq" is in the form "yufa'" from waqa yaqi, like "wazana yazinu." Abu Haywa recited "yuwawwiq" with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the qaf. "Al-muflihun" means those who achieve success in their aim.

People differed concerning the Most High's words: ﴿And those who came after them﴾. Al-Farra' said: It means the third group of the Companions, those who embraced Islam or matured at the end of the Prophet's (ﷺ) lifetime. The majority of scholars said: It means those who come from the Successors and others until the Day of Resurrection. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, described the saying that every person who is not from the first generation should adopt. As for the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "alladhina," it is in the nominative case as a conjunction with "hum" (them), or with "walladhina" (and those who), or it is nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. The Most High's words, "yaqulun" (they say), form a circumstantial clause (hal) that carries a benefit. The meaning is: "And those who came saying such-and-such." Or "yaqulun" may be a descriptive clause (sifah).

The Most High said:

﴿And those who had settled in the abode [of faith] and in belief before them love those who emigrate to them, and find no need in their breasts for what they have been given, and prefer them over themselves, even though they themselves are in need. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful.﴾ ﴿And those who came after them say: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and put no resentment in our hearts toward those who believe. Our Lord, You are indeed Kind and Merciful."﴾

"Alladhina tabawwa'u" (those who settled) refers to the Ansar (the Helpers of Madina). The pronoun in "qablihim" (before them) refers to the Muhajirun (the Emigrants). "Al-dar" (the abode) is Madina. The meaning is: they settled in the abode together with belief, and with this connection the meaning of the Most High's words "min qablihim" (before them) is correct, so reflect on it. Belief is not something one can "settle in," because it is not a place. But this is from eloquent speech, and it can be explained in several ways, all of which are beautiful and good.

In this verse Allah the Most High praised the Ansar for loving the Muhajirun, may Allah be pleased with all of them, for preferring them over themselves, and for having been protected from the stinginess of their own souls. This is because the implication of the Most High's words, ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful﴾, is that these praised people have been protected from stinginess.

"Al-hajah" (need) here means envy. This was said by al-Hasan. It then covers all the aspects that are contrary to what the Prophet (ﷺ) did in giving the Muhajirun the wealth of Bani al-Nadir and the villages. "Utu" (were given) means "were given." The raised pronoun in "utu," whose subject is not named, refers to the Muhajirun.

The Most High's words, ﴿and prefer them over themselves﴾, up to the end of the verse, describe the Ansar. It has been narrated, through more than one chain, that it was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar. Abu al-Mutawakkil said: he was Thabit ibn Qays. Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said in the book of Makki: the kunya (honorific nickname) of this man was Abu Talha. Al-Mahdawi confused the account of this man: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called for hosting an emigrant, and an Ansari responded, though he had no wealth. He took the guest away and said to his wife, 'This is the guest of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' She said, 'By Allah, I have nothing except the food of the children.' He said to her, 'Put your children to sleep, extinguish the lamp, and offer what you have to the guest, and let him think that we are eating.' They did that, and when he went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the morning, he said, 'Allah was amazed at your deed last night,' and the verse was revealed concerning that."

I found him and said, "Shall I give you a drink?" He gestured yes. Then a man was crying "Ah!" My cousin gestured that I should go to him. It was Hisham ibn al-'As. I said, "Will you drink?" Then another was saying "Ah!" Hisham gestured that I should go to him. I came to him and found that his soul had departed. I returned to Hisham and found that he had died. The stinginess of the soul is a poverty that the wealth of money does not remove; rather, it increases it and makes it worse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 59, verses 11–13:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Have you not considered those who committed hypocrisy, saying to their brothers who disbelieved among the People of the Scripture: "If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you, and we will never obey anyone against you, and if you are fought, we will surely support you." And Allah testifies that they are liars.﴾ ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go out with them; and if they are fought, they will not support them; and if they do support them, they will surely turn their backs; then they will not be aided.﴾ ﴿Indeed, you are more fearsome in their breasts than Allah. That is because they are a people who do not comprehend.﴾

This verse was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Rifa'a ibn al-Tabut, and a group of the hypocrites of the Ansar, who had sent to the Banu al-Nadir and said to them: "Hold firm in your strongholds, for we are with you, however your circumstances turn." They only intended by this that their souls would be strengthened, hoping they would hold out, so that Muhammad ﷺ would not be able to prevail over them, and their aim would be accomplished. They were liars in what they said of that, and for this reason they did not go out when the Banu al-Nadir were expelled, but remained in their homes. His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And if they support them﴾ means: if they attempt to support them, they will be defeated, and then Allah, Exalted is He, will not give victory to any of them.

The verbs in His saying, "they will not go out" (lā yakhrujūna) and "they will not support them" (lā yanṣurūnahum), were not put in the jussive mood, because they are construed according to the ruling of the oath (al-qasam) and not according to the ruling of the condition (al-shart). Yet there is scrutiny in this.

Then Exalted is He addressed the community of Muhammad ﷺ, informing them that the Jews and the hypocrites are more fearful of the believers than of Allah, Exalted is He, because they anticipate the immediate evil from the believers and do not believe in the deferred punishment from Allah, Exalted is He. That is due to their lack of understanding of matters and their lack of success in reaching the truth.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 59, verses 14–17:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿They will not fight you all together, except in fortified towns or from behind walls. Their violence among themselves is severe. You think them united, but their hearts are divided. That is because they are a people who do not reason.﴾ ﴿Like those before them, shortly before, who tasted the evil consequence of their affair; and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Like the Shaytan (Satan) when he says to man, "Disbelieve." But when he disbelieves, he says, "Indeed, I am free of you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿So the end of both will be that they are in the Fire, abiding eternally therein. And that is the recompense of the wrongdoers.﴾

The pronoun in His saying, "They will not fight you," refers to the Banu al-Nadir and all the Jews. This is the view of a group of the exegetes. It is also possible that it means the Jews and the hypocrites, since the inclusion of the hypocrites in His saying, ﴿Their violence among themselves is severe. You think them united, but their hearts are divided﴾, is clear and firmly established. The meaning of the verse is: they will not fight you as an army in open ground. "Al-qura" (fortified towns) means cities. Al-Farra' said: this is an irregular plural. Al-Zajjaj said: what is in the Qur'an is not irregular; it is like ḍay'a and ḍiya'.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and many of the Meccan readers recited "jiddan" (ﺟِدًا), in the sense of a collective noun. Many of the Meccan readers and Harun, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, recited "jud" (جُدْ) with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the dal, and its meaning is the base of a structure, like a wall or the like. The remaining readers recited "judur" (جُدُرٌ) with a damma on the jim and the dal, which is the plural of jidar (wall). Abu Raja' and Abu Haywa recited "judr" (جُدْرٌ) with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the dal, which is a lightening of the plural of jidar. It is possible that it means the "judur" of palm trees, i.e. from behind their palm groves, since these are used as protection in times of siege.

His saying, ﴿Their violence among themselves is severe﴾, means: in their hostility and their mutual affection (?). In the reading of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "You think them united, but their hearts are more divided" (ashanna). This is the state of disunited groups, which are always defeated in whatever they attempt. The word is derived from "shatat" (dispersion), which is separation and the like.

His saying, ﴿Like those before them﴾, means: their example is like the example of those before them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: they are the Banu Qaynuqa', because the Prophet (ﷺ) expelled them from Madinah before the Banu al-Nadir, and they were an example for them. Qatada and Mujahid said: "those before them" are the disbelievers of the Battle of Badr; they came before them and were an example for them in being overcome and subdued. Some interpreters said: the pronoun in His saying, ﴿Like those before them﴾, refers to the hypocrites, namely the hypocrites of earlier nations; because they were defeated and humiliation befell them throughout time, so they are an example for these. But His saying, "shortly before" (qarīban), either refers to the time of Musa, peace be upon him, otherwise this interpretation is weakened, unless "qarīban" is made an adverbial complement of "tasted", so that the meaning is: they tasted the evil consequence of their affair shortly after their disobedience and its recentness; and the meaning is not that the example is recent in time relative to the one it exemplifies. In every interpretation, "qarīban" is either an adverb or an adjective of an adverb. "Al-wabal" means severity, what is disliked, and the evil consequence. "The painful punishment" is in the Hereafter.

His saying, "Like the Shaytan," means: the example of these two groups, the hypocrites and the Banu al-Nadir, is like the example of the Shaytan and the human being. The hypocrites are exemplified by the Shaytan, and the Banu al-Nadir are exemplified by the human being. Mujahid and the majority of the interpreters held that "al-shaytan" and "al-insan" in this verse are generic nouns, because it is the custom that this is done by "shayatin" with "nas", just as the Shaytan misleads the human being and then flees from him after he has entangled him. Likewise, the hypocrites misled the Banu al-Nadir, incited them to stand firm and promised them victory. But when the Banu al-Nadir betrayed and revealed their faces, the hypocrites left them in the worst condition. Some of the narrators of stories held that this refers to a specific shaytan, and al-Zajjaj mentioned that his name was Barsisa. They said: he entrusted a woman [with something], and it was said: she was brought to him so that he might cure her of madness by his supplication. The Shaytan then made it attractive to him to have intercourse with her; she became pregnant, and he feared disgrace. The Shaytan then made it attractive to him to kill her and bury her; he did so, and then he publicized it. When the woman was extracted and the worshipper was carried with the worst carrying, while he had said, "She died and I stood over her and buried her," and when she was found murdered, they knew his lie. The Shaytan then confronted him and said to him: "Disbelieve, and prostrate to me, and I will save you." He did so, and then abandoned him at that point and said: "Indeed, I am free of you." All of this is a weak report. The first interpretation is the intended meaning of the speech. The saying of the Shaytan, "Indeed I fear Allah," is ostentation and show-off; it is not his belief, and he does not know Allah with true knowledge of Him, and his fear does not restrain him from any evil that he brings upon the son of Adam from first to last.

His saying, ﴿So the end of both﴾, the verse: the pronoun may refer to the two specific individuals mentioned, and it may refer to the two generic nouns, i.e. this is the end of every shaytan and human being whose affair is like this. Al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd recited "'aqibatuhuma" (عاقِبَتُهُما) with a damma, and the majority recited "'aqibatahuma" (عاقِبَتَهُما) with a fatha. The position of "anna" differs from the case-ending of "al-'aqiba" in the two readings. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash recited "khalidani" (خالِدانِ) with a damma, on the basis that it is the predicate of "anna", and the adverbial phrase is cancelled. This reading is subject to the objection of cancelling the adverbial phrase twice, as al-Farra' said, but this is permissible according to Sibawayh as an emphasis.

The companions of Paradise are the attainers of success.﴾ ﴿If We had sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from fear of Allah. So Allah, exalted is He, punished them by making them forget themselves. Sufyan said: the meaning is: the share of their own selves. The wording of this verse implies that whoever knows his self and does not forget it knows his Lord, glory be to Him. It is narrated from him that he, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Know yourself and you will know your Lord." Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 59, verse 22–24:

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed. He is the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.﴾ ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the King, the Pure (al-Quddus), the Source of Peace (al-Salam), the Giver of Security (al-Mu'min), the Guardian (al-Muhaymin), the Mighty, the Compeller (al-Jabbar), the Supreme (al-Mutakabbir). Glory be to Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner. To Him belong the most beautiful names. Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

When He said, ﴿from the fear of Allah﴾ [al-Hashr: 21], He brought the attributes that make this fear necessary for His creatures. "Al-Ghayb" (the unseen) is what is hidden from the created beings, and "al-Shahadah" (the witnessed) is what they have witnessed. Harb al-Makki said: al-Ghayb is the Hereafter and al-Shahadah is the world.

The majority of people read "al-Quddus" with a ḍammah on the qaf. It is a verb from taqaddasa, meaning he purified himself. The "ḥazīrat al-quds" (the sacred enclosure) is Paradise because it is pure. From the same root come "Rūḥ al-Quds" (the Holy Spirit) and "al-Arḍ al-Muqaddasah" (the Holy Land), Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is narrated from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he read "al-Quddus" with a fatḥah on the qaf, and this is also a dialect (lughah).

"Al-Salam" means: the one who is free from injustice (sullima min jawrihi). This is a name with an elided genitive, meaning dhu al-salam (the Possessor of Peace), because belief in Him, His unification, and His acts are all peace for the one who believes.

"Al-Mu'min" is an active participle from "amana," in the sense of "amman" (granting security). Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab said its meaning is: the one who confirms the believers in their having believed. An-Nahhas said: or in their testimony about people on the Day of Resurrection. Some of the interpreters said: its meaning is: the one who affirms Himself in His eternal words, there is no deity other than Him.

"Al-Muhaymin" means: the trustworthy and the Preserver. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Mu'arraj said: al-Muhaymin means the witness, in the language of Quraysh. This is a pattern (binā') that occurs in attributes only in muhaymin, musaytir, mubayqir and mubayṭir, and in names it occurs in "muḥaymir" (the name of a valley) and "mudaybir".

"Al-Jabbar" is the one to whom nothing is comparable and who does not reach His rank. From it comes "nakhlah jabbarah" (a towering palm tree) when it is out of reach. Az-Zahrawi recited:

"They circled around it at the time of its picking,
and returned water to it until it was restored (tujabbara)."

"Al-Mutakabbir" means: the one to whom pride (takabbur) truly belongs.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, declared Himself free from the polytheism of the disbelievers, who associate with Him idols that possess none of these attributes. "Al-Bari'" means the Creator: Allah originated (bara'a) creation, that is, brought them into existence. "Al-Musawwir" is the One who gives forms. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, read "al-Musawwir" with the active construction applied to "al-Bari'" in it, and this is a good reading, intended to mean the beautiful in forms. Some people reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he read "al-Musawwar" with a fatḥah on the waw and a kasrah on the ra', according to their saying "al-ḥasan al-wajh" (beautiful of face).

His statement, ﴿To Him belong the most beautiful names﴾, means: possessing beauty in their meanings, which subsist in His Essence, there is no deity but Him. These are the names that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ enumerated in his saying: "Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one; whoever enumerates them enters Paradise." Al-Tirmidhi and others narrated them with chains (musnadah), and the narrators differed concerning some of them, and nothing has been authenticated regarding them except the counting of them without specifying them. The rest of the verse is clear.

The commentary on Surah [al-Hashr] is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
